w: For close to 500 years, from the Eighteenth Dynasty through the Twentieth, pharaohs and nobles were buried in tombs cut into this wadi's rock face on the Nile's west bank. Sixty-five tombs are known today, ranging from a simple pit to KV5's sprawling complex of over 120 chambers, built for the sons of Ramesses II.
s: Sixty-five tombs cut into one royal valley
_facts: Rock-cut royal tombs excavated over nearly 500 years, 18th to 20th Dynasty, on the Nile's west bank opposite Thebes
65 known tombs and chambers, from the simple pit KV54 to the 120-plus-chamber KV5
Principal burial place for New Kingdom pharaohs and privileged nobles

w: Construction here began under Senusret I around 1971 BC and never stopped, continuing into the Ptolemaic era. The ancient Egyptians called it Ipet-isut, the most select of places, main house of worship for Amun, head of the Theban Triad. UNESCO listed it in 1979 with the rest of Thebes.
s: Nearly two thousand years of temple-building
_facts: Vast temple complex begun under Senusret I (r. 1971-1926 BC), construction continuing into the Ptolemaic period
Known to the ancient Egyptians as Ipet-isut; main place of worship for Amun and the Theban Triad
Added to the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1979 as part of the city of Thebes

w: Giovanni Belzoni forced his way into this tomb on 16 October 1817 and found one of the most heavily decorated burial places in the valley, also one of the largest and deepest. It picked up nicknames over the years, including Belzoni's Tomb and the Tomb of Apis, clues to how it was understood before Egyptology existed.
s: The deepest, most decorated tomb in the valley
_facts: Tomb of Pharaoh Seti I of the Nineteenth Dynasty, known as KV17
Discovered by Giovanni Belzoni on 16 October 1817
One of the largest and deepest tombs in the Valley of the Kings; also called Belzoni's Tomb

w: The mortuary temple of Ramesses III is the best-preserved building near the foot of the Theban Hills, famous for carved reliefs of the pharaoh's defeat of the mysterious Sea Peoples around 1175 BC. A Coptic settlement called Jeme grew up around it afterward and lasted until the 9th century, reusing its stones.
s: Where Ramesses III carved his victory into stone
_facts: Archaeological site on Luxor's West Bank, dominated by the Mortuary Temple of Ramesses III
Reliefs depict Ramesses III's defeat of the Sea Peoples, including the Battle of the Delta, c. 1186-1155 BC
A Coptic settlement, Jeme, occupied the site until the 9th century

w: Archaeologists only began digging this site in late 2020, and what they found stopped them in their tracks, a city so well preserved that people started comparing it to Pompeii. Named after the sun god Aten, it appears to be the largest city of its kind found from ancient Egypt, hidden under sand for three millennia.
_facts: Ancient Egyptian city remains on the west bank of the Nile near Luxor, excavation began late 2020
Named after the sun god Aten; emerging as the largest city of its kind found in ancient Egypt
Remarkable state of preservation drew comparisons to Pompeii

w: Built across the river from Thebes as a memorial to the New Kingdom pharaoh Seti I, this temple sits in the Theban Necropolis near the town of Qurna, a quieter counterpart to the grander mortuary temples nearby. It shares its builder with one of the most decorated tombs in the Valley of the Kings, just over the hill.
s: A pharaoh's memorial temple, tucked beside Qurna
_facts: Memorial (mortuary) temple of Pharaoh Seti I of the New Kingdom
Located in the Theban Necropolis, Upper Egypt, near the town of Qurna, across the Nile from Luxor

w: Perched on the corniche with the Nile's east bank spread out below it, this archaeological museum gathers artefacts pulled from the temples and tombs of ancient Thebes. It is a compact counterpoint to the sprawl of Karnak and the Valley of the Kings, everything condensed into one building you can walk in an afternoon.
s: Antiquities on the corniche, overlooking the Nile
_facts: Archaeological museum in Luxor, standing on the corniche overlooking the Nile's east bank

w: Victor Loret discovered this undecorated tomb in 1898, burial place of Tia'a, wife of Amenhotep II and mother of Thutmose IV. Workmen digging the nearby tomb of Siptah later broke into a side chamber by accident. Excavators recovered fragments of her canopic chest, along with shabtis bearing her name.
s: A queen found by accident by another tomb's diggers
_facts: Tomb KV32, burial site of Tia'a, wife of Amenhotep II and mother of Thutmose IV
Discovered in 1898 by Victor Loret; undecorated tomb running about 40 metres into the hillside
Workmen excavating the nearby tomb of Siptah (KV47) accidentally broke into it
